flags.detail: The key (C, std::terminate) is right for the ordinary case, but the rule the explanation states to justify it is false as written: "Since C++11 a destructor with no explicit exception specification is implicitly noexcept." That is not unconditional. Per [except.spec], a destructor without a noexcept-specifier is potentially-throwing if any destructor of a potentially-constructed subobject is potentially-throwing. So a user-provided destructor that carries no exception specification of its own can still be noexcept(false) by inheritance from a member or base. Verified with g++ 13.3 -std=c++17. Program 1: `struct A { ~A() { throw 1; } }; int main(){ try { A a; } catch(int){ cout << "caught"; } }` — compiler warns "-Wterminate: throw will always call terminate", runs, prints "terminate called after throwing an instance of 'int'", aborts (exit 134). Program 2, identical except A gains a member with a throwing destructor: `struct M { ~M() noexcept(false) {} }; struct A { M m; ~A() { throw 1; } };` — same main, compiles with no -Wterminate warning, prints "caught" then "end", exit 0. A third program confirms the mechanism: std::is_nothrow_destructible<A>::value is false for the A that holds M, true for an A with a plain member. So in program 2 the destructor has no exception specification of its own, yet option A's outcome (propagates and is caught) is what actually happens — the stem as worded does not exclude that case. Fix the explanation to say the implicit specification is noexcept *unless a base or member destructor is potentially-throwing*, and tighten the stem to something like "...a destructor that carries no exception specification of its own, in a class all of whose bases and members have non-throwing destructors".
flags.suggested: Key stays C. Explanation sentence should read: "Since C++11 a destructor with no explicit exception specification is implicitly noexcept unless some base-class or member destructor is itself potentially-throwing, so here the escaping exception crosses a noexcept boundary and std::terminate runs...". Stem should pin that no subobject destructor is declared noexcept(false).

flags.detail: Key C (operator->) is correct and the reserved list given (::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof, typeid, alignof) is accurate. The problem is the reason attached to it: "because each one either operates on a name or a type rather than on a value, so there is no operand for a user-defined function to receive". That claim is asserted over the whole list and is plainly false for two of its members. The conditional operator ?: takes three ordinary value operands and has no name or type operand at all; the pointer-to-member operator .* takes an object expression on the left and a pointer-to-member *value* on the right, both of which a function could perfectly well receive. (The real reasons differ per operator: ?: has short-circuit evaluation semantics the language declines to hand to a user function, and .* / . are withheld to keep member access meaning one fixed thing.) A student who internalises the stated rationale will mis-derive which operators are overloadable — note that ->* and -> , which also involve member access, *are* overloadable, so the rationale does not even separate the two groups. Verified in passing with g++ 13.3 -std=c++17 that `B operator.(B);` is rejected at parse ("expected type-specifier before '.' token"), and that repeated application of a user-defined operator-> chains correctly through two levels to a real pointer, which is the part of the explanation that is right.
flags.suggested: Key stays C. Replace the causal clause with a non-explanatory one, e.g. "The other three are on the short fixed list the language declines to make overloadable — ::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof, typeid and alignof — while -> and even ->* are overloadable." Drop the "operates on a name or a type" justification entirely.

flags.detail: GEN-T2U1-015 and GEN-T2U1-028 test the identical proposition, reworded. 015's key B leads with "Declaring any constructor of its own suppresses the implicitly declared default constructor"; 028's key B is "Declaring any constructor stops the compiler from implicitly declaring a default constructor." Both stems are the same scenario — a class gains a parameterised constructor, an object declaration that needs the default constructor stops compiling — with 015 wrapping it in an array declaration and 028 in a plain object declaration. Verified both diagnose the same way under g++ 13.3 -std=c++17: `struct Item { Item(int); }; Item shelf[5];` gives "no matching function for call to 'Item::Item()'", and `struct Point { int a,b; Point(int,int); }; Point p;` gives "no matching function for call to 'Point::Point()'" — literally the same error, same cause. Both are in this one 34-question batch, so a student meets the same fact twice. The leaf tags differ (015 sits on memory allocation, 028 on constructors and destructors) but the discriminating knowledge does not. Keep 028, which sits on the more natural leaf and whose distractor set (aggregate-ness, implicit deletion) is the sharper one, and re-aim 015 at a fact it does not share — e.g. the array-of-class-type angle proper (why `Item shelf[5] = {Item(1),...}` works, which I confirmed compiles, versus `std::vector<Item> v(5)` also failing for the same missing default constructor while `v.reserve(5)` succeeds), or move it onto dynamic array allocation.
flags.suggested: Keep GEN-T2U1-028 as written. Rewrite GEN-T2U1-015 so its key is not "a user-declared constructor suppresses the implicit default constructor" — or drop it.

notes: All 34 reviewed; every question turning on exact language behaviour was compiled and run under g++ 13.3 -std=c++17 rather than recalled — 012 (prints 4, key C confirmed), 014 (prints 'ed', key B), 020 (prints 12 with -Wreorder, key C), 021 (prints 1, key A), 015 (both the failing array and the brace-initialised remedy), 022 (rejected: "invalid constructor; you probably meant 'X (const X&)'"), 024 (all four sub-cases of explicit), 025 ("mem-initializer for 'Widget::count' follows constructor delegation"), 028, 030, 031, 033 (f('a') fine, f(7L) ambiguous), 034, 013, 010 (both the link error and the C++17 inline remedy), 019 (real multiple-definition link failure across two TUs), 003 (private inheritance overriding a virtual while both t.pub() and Buffer& b = t are rejected), 011, 023 (std::move on a destructor-owning class silently copies the raw pointer), 017/018 (sizeof 1/1/8), and the two UB cases 016 and 026, which both crash as expected. The keys are right on all 34 — I found no wrong key and no distractor that survives the stem. The three defects are all of the softer kind: one explanation stating an implicitly-noexcept rule more broadly than it holds (027, and I built the counterexample that flips the answer to option A), one explanation offering a false causal rationale for a correct list (029), and one genuine within-batch duplicate of the suppressed-default-constructor fact (015 vs 028).
